kf1.tip: Choose a natural event near where you live. Decide whether it is a natural hazard or just a phenomenon, and whether it is geological or meteorological.
kf1.note: A strong answer names one real event and then makes two separate decisions. First, does it threaten people or property? If it does, it is a hazard. If it would happen with nobody affected, it is just a phenomenon. Second, is it caused by Earth processes (geological, like a landslide) or by weather and climate (meteorological, like a flood)? If you called it a hazard without saying who or what it threatens, the answer is incomplete.

kf2.tip: Sketch from memory a labelled diagram linking heat in the core, convection currents in the mantle and the tectonic plates, with arrows showing which way each moves.
kf2.note: A good sketch shows a heat source at the core with arrows rising through the mantle. The arrows turn sideways beneath the plates, then sink again where the rock has cooled, forming a loop. Label the plates on top, with arrows showing them dragged along by the moving mantle. Check that your labels say hot rock rises and cool rock sinks. If your arrows never connect to the plates, you have missed the point of the diagram.

cs1.tip: Suppose the pressure on the inner core fell while its heat stayed the same. Predict what state it would be in, and what seismologists would then detect.
cs1.note: The inner core would most likely become liquid. It stays solid only because extreme pressure forces its atoms into a solid lattice, even though it is hotter than the outer core. Remove that pressure and heat would win. Seismologists would then stop detecting the waves that only travel through solids, because those waves could no longer pass through the inner core. If you said it would stay solid, you have forgotten that pressure, not temperature, keeps it solid.
